claim: 17 healthy human participants (nine females, age: mean ± s.d.=29.29 ± 4.5 y) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision took part in the study.
source: 17 healthy human participants (nine females, age: mean ± s.d.=29.29 ± 4.5 y) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision took part in the study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant demographics in the study.

claim: For a medium effect size of 0.3 and a power of 0.8, a minimum number of 16 participants was needed.
source: For a medium effect size of 0.3 and a power of 0.8, we needed a minimum number of 16 participants.
evidence: This is a power analysis calculation reported in the methods.

claim: Data collection was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences, Tehran.
source: Data collection was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences, Tehran.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: The behavioral data for two participants was not correctly saved during the scanning due to technical problems.
source: The behavioral data for two participants was not correctly saved during the scanning due to technical problems.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data collection issues.

claim: The experiment used object stimuli from four categories: human bodies, cars, houses, and cats.
source: To determine the effect of target-distractor similarity on attentional modulation, we used object stimuli from four categories (human bodies, cars, houses, and cats).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Body and house categories were included because there are regions in the brain that are highly responsive and unresponsive to each of these categories.
source: We included body and house categories because there are regions in the brain that are highly responsive and unresponsive to each of these categories, which provided us with a range of responsiveness in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for category selection.

claim: The two remaining categories (cars and cats) were chosen based on previous behavioral results to include categories that provided a range of similarities.
source: We chose the two remaining categories based on previous behavioral results to include categories that provided us with a range of similarities (Xu and Vaziri-Pashkam, 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous work as justification.

claim: The experiment consisted of 16 conditions: 4 isolated conditions and 12 paired conditions.
source: Thus, the experiment consisted of 16 conditions: 4 isolated conditions in which isolated stimuli from one of the four categories were presented, and 12 paired conditions (six category pairs × two attentional targets for each pair) in which a target stimulus from the cued category was superimposed with a distractor stimulus from another category for all category combinations.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Each category consisted of 10 exemplars all varying in identity, 3D-orientation (for houses and cars), and pose (for bodies and cats).
source: Each category consisted of 10 exemplars all varying in identity, 3D-orientation (for houses and cars), and pose (for bodies and cats, see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Images were presented at the center of the screen on a gray background, subtending 10.2° of visual angle.
source: Images were presented at the center of the screen on a gray background, subtending 10.2o of visual angle.
evidence: This is a direct statement about stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: A red fixation point subtending 0.45° of visual angle was presented at the center of the screen throughout the run.
source: A red fixation point subtending 0.45o of visual angle was presented at the center of the screen throughout the run (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participants performed a one-back repetition detection task on the cued category by pressing the response button when the same stimulus from the attended category appeared in two consecutive trials.
source: During the block, participants maintained attention on the images from the cued category, and performed a one-back repetition detection task on them by pressing the response button when the same stimulus from the attended category appeared in two consecutive trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental task.

claim: Repetition occurred two to three times at random times in each block.
source: Repetition occurred two to three times at random times in each block.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design.

claim: Each block lasted for 10 s, starting with the cue word presented for 1 s, followed by 1 s of fixation.
source: Each block lasted for 10 s, starting with the cue word presented for 1 s, followed by 1 s of fixation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of experimental blocks.

claim: Each image was presented for 400 ms, followed by 400ms of fixation.
source: Each image was presented for 400 ms, followed by 400ms of fixation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 10 participants completed 16 runs and 7 participants completed 12 runs of the main experiment.
source: 10 participants completed 16 runs and 7 participants completed 12 runs of the main experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of runs completed by participants.

claim: The study investigated five different regions of interest (ROIs): LO, pFs, EBA, PPA, and V1.
source: Considering that we used object categories, we investigated five different regions of interest (ROIs): the object-selective areas lateral occipital cortex (LO) and posterior fusiform gyrus (pFs) as general object-selective regions, the body-selective extrastriate body area (EBA) and the scene-selective parahippocampal place area (PPA) as regions that are highly selective for specific categories, and the primary visual cortex (V1) as a control region.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ROIs examined in the study.

claim: These regions were chosen because they could all be consistently defined in both hemispheres of all participants and included a large number of voxels.
source: We chose these regions because they could all be consistently defined in both hemispheres of all participants and included a large number of voxels.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for ROI selection.

claim: Meridian mapping was used to localize the primary visual cortex V1.
source: We used meridian mapping to localize the primary visual cortex V1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method used to localize V1.

claim: Data of 10 participants were recorded using the Siemens 3T Tim Trio MRI system with a 32-channel head coil at the Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM).
source: We recorded the data of 10 participants using the Siemens 3T Tim Trio MRI system with a 32-channel head coil at the Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the MRI system used for data collection.

claim: Data of seven additional participants were collected on a Siemens Prisma MRI system using a 64-channel head coil at the National Brain-mapping Laboratory (NBML).
source: We collected the data of seven additional participants on a Siemens Prisma MRI system using a 64-channel head coil at the National Brain-mapping Laboratory (NBML).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the MRI system used for data collection.

claim: For the functional scans, 33 slices parallel to the AC-PC line were acquired using T2*-weighted gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequences covering the whole brain.
source: For the functional scans, including the main experiment and the localizer experiments, we acquired 33 slices parallel to the AC-PC line using T2*-weighted gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequences covering the whole brain (TR=2 s, TE=30 ms, flip angle=90o, voxel size=3 × 3 × 3 mm3, matrix size = 64 × 64).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: No spatial smoothing was performed on the data.
source: We performed no spatial smoothing on the data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: The first four volumes (8 s) of each run were eliminated to avoid the initial magnetization transient.
source: We eliminated the first four volumes (8 s) of each run to avoid the initial magnetization transient.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: Participants had an average detection rate of 90.49% across all runs.
source: Participants had an average detection rate of 90.49% across all runs, confirming effective attention towards the cued stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed effect of attention was limited to higher-level visual areas.
source: Thus, the observed effect was limited to higher-level visual areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical results showing effects in higher-level ROIs but not V1.

claim: For stimuli that elicit more different responses, attention causes a greater response modulation, while the shift of attention between stimuli with more similar responses causes little response change.
source: These results demonstrate that for stimuli that elicit more different responses, attention causes a greater response modulation, while the shift of attention between stimuli with more similar responses causes little response change.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis between univariate shift and category distance.

claim: Less significant results in PPA might arise from the fact that this region shows no response to body and cat stimuli and little response to car stimuli.
source: Less significant results in PPA might arise from the fact that this region shows no response to body and cat stimuli and little response to car stimuli (see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement providing an explanation for the PPA results.

claim: The response gain model predicts a multiplicative scaling of responses through which neural responses are increased by a gain factor.
source: The response gain model predicts a multiplicative scaling of responses through which neural responses are increased by a gain factor (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the response gain model, supported by citations.

claim: The tuning sharpening model proposes that attentional enhancement depends on the neuronal tuning for the attended stimulus, leading to an increase in response for optimal stimuli, and little increase in response or even response suppression for non-optimal stimuli.
source: The tuning sharpening model, instead, proposes that attentional enhancement depends on the neuronal tuning for the attended stimulus, leading to an increase in response for optimal stimuli, and little increase in response or even response suppression for non-optimal stimuli (Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the tuning sharpening model, supported by a citation.

claim: The empirically-observed relationship between attentional enhancement and target-distractor similarity are predicted by the tuning sharpening model, but not the response gain model.
source: We find that the empirically-observed relationship between attentional enhancement and target-distractor similarity are predicted by the tuning sharpening model, but not the response gain model.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation results.

claim: The response gain model predicted no relationship between univariate shift and category distance in either population.
source: We found that the response gain model predicted no relationship between univariate shift and category distance in either population (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The tuning sharpening model predicted a positive correlation between univariate shift and category distance in both neural populations.
source: In contrast, the tuning sharpening model predicted a positive correlation between univariate shift and category distance in both neural populations (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: The response gain model predicted no relationship between attentional weight shift and category distance.
source: Here, too, we find that the response gain model predicted no relationship between attentional weight shift and category distance (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: The tuning sharpening model predicted a positive relationship between weight shift and category distance for both neural populations.
source: In contrast, the tuning sharpening model predicted a positive relationship between weight shift and category distance for both neural populations (Figure 8C–D), providing further evidence for tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism for attentional enhancement.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: The labeled line model could predict the positive correlation between the univariate shift and category distance in a region with high selectivity for a certain category, but it failed to predict the results in other cases.
source: Although the labeled line model could predict the positive correlation between the univariate shift and category distance in a region with high selectivity for a certain category, it failed to predict the results in other cases (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the labeled line model's predictions.

claim: The tuning model predicts the empirically-observed effect of target-distractor similarity on attentional effects both at the univariate and at the multivariate level, while the response gain model does not.
source: In sum, the tuning model predicts the empirically-observed effect of target-distractor similarity on attentional effects both at the univariate and at the multivariate level, while the response gain model does not.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the simulation results.

claim: Visual stimuli compete with each other for cortical processing and attention biases this competition in favor of the attended stimulus.
source: Visual stimuli compete with each other for cortical processing and attention biases this competition in favor of the attended stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing the theoretical framework.

claim: The strength of the attentional bias toward the target decreases with increasing target-distractor similarity.
source: We demonstrated that the strength of the attentional bias toward the target is not fixed but decreases with increasing target-distractor similarity.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main finding.

claim: Simulations provided evidence that the result pattern is explained by tuning sharpening rather than an increase in gain.
source: Simulations provided evidence that this result pattern is explained by tuning sharpening rather than an increase in gain.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing the simulation results.

claim: The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral effects of target-distractor similarity on attentional biases.
source: Our findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral effects of target-distractor similarity on attentional biases and suggest tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism in object-based attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the implications of the findings.

claim: Tuning sharpening is suggested as the underlying mechanism in object-based attention.
source: Our findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral effects of target-distractor similarity on attentional biases and suggest tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism in object-based attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the proposed mechanism.

claim: Different stimuli compete for cortical representation and processing due to the brain's limited neural resources.
source: Since processing all the incoming information is impossible due to the brain's limited neural resources, different stimuli compete for cortical representation and processing (Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Kastner et al., 1998; Reynolds et al., 1999; Beck and Kastner, 2005; Reddy et al., 2009; McMains and Kastner, 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Attention enhances the response related to the attended stimulus by approximately 30% compared to its response when unattended.
source: Evidence from electrophysiology and fMRI studies have demonstrated the role of attention in biasing the competition by enhancing the response related to the attended stimulus by approximately 30% compared to its response when unattended, in both electrophysiology studies of the monkey brain (Treue and Maunsell, 1996; Reynolds et al., 1999; Treue and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds and Desimone, 2003; Fallah et al., 2007) and fMRI studies of the human brain (Reddy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Competition between stimuli is content-dependent, with higher competition between stimuli that are located closer to each other or between stimuli with more similar cortical representation patterns.
source: Behavioral studies indicate that the competition between stimuli is content-dependent (Cohen et al., 2014), with higher competition between stimuli that are located closer to each other (Franconeri et al., 2013), or between stimuli with more similar cortical representation patterns (Cohen et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lower performance for more similar target-distractor pairs is due to the fact that the neural resources needed for detailed processing are shared to a greater extent.
source: Furthermore, behavioral studies on the effect of target-distractor similarity on performance have proposed that lower performance for more similar target-distractor pairs is due to the fact that the neural resources needed for detailed processing are shared to a greater extent (Cohen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: A direct neuroscientific investigation of how target-distractor similarity affects visual representations, and a mechanistic explanation of how shared resources affect attentional biases are missing.
source: However, a direct neuroscientific investigation of how target-distractor similarity affects visual representations, and a mechanistic explanation of how shared resources affect attentional biases are missing.
evidence: This is a direct statement identifying a gap in the literature.

claim: The response gain model predicts that attention scales the neurons' tuning function without affecting its shape.
source: Therefore, the response gain model predicts that attention scales the neurons' tuning function without affecting its shape (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The tuning sharpening model predicts that attention causes a sharpening of the neurons' tuning function, with a sharp increase in the response to optimal stimuli, and no increase in the response to the non-optimal stimuli.
source: Therefore, this model predicts that attention causes a sharpening of the neurons' tuning function, with a sharp increase in the response to optimal stimuli, and no increase in the response to the non-optimal stimuli (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The study reveals the neural basis of the attentional effect graded by target-distractor similarity in the human brain both at the univariate level and at the multivariate level.
source: Using stimuli from four object categories, our study reveals the neural basis of the attentional effect graded by target-distractor similarity in the human brain both at the univariate level and at the multivariate level.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main finding.

claim: In the competition between multiple stimuli, the attentional bias is not constant.
source: First, our results show that in the competition between multiple stimuli, the attentional bias is not constant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the main finding.

claim: Previous studies have shown attentional modulation in the human brain as an average value without considering its variance for different pairings of targets and distractors.
source: Previous studies have shown attentional modulation in the human brain as an average value without considering its variance for different pairings of targets and distractors (Reddy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: The attentional bias offers less advantage for a more similar target-distractor pair.
source: We refine our understanding by showing that however, the attentional bias offers less advantage for a more similar target-distractor pair.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main finding.

claim: The finding provides direct neural evidence for the adverse effects of target-distractor similarity on performance, as previously reported in behavioral studies.
source: Second, this finding provides direct neural evidence for the adverse effects of target-distractor similarity on performance, as previously reported in behavioral studies (Cohen et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implications of the finding, supported by citations.

claim: The reduction in performance is because the representation of the target (relative to the distractor) is less effectively enhanced by attention when the target becomes more similar to the distractor.
source: Our results demonstrate that this reduction in performance is because the representation of the target (relative to the distractor) is less effectively enhanced by attention when the target becomes more similar to the distractor.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mechanistic explanation for behavioral effects.

claim: Evidence on the effect of attention on V1 responses is divergent, with some previous neuroimaging studies showing a significant effect of attention on neural responses, while others report no significant effect of attention.
source: Evidence on the effect of attention on V1 responses is divergent, with some previous neuroimaging studies showing a significant effect of attention on neural responses (Somers et al., 1999; Gandhi et al., 1999), while others report no significant effect of attention (Corbetta et al., 1990; Thorat and Peelen, 2022; Doostani et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The apparent discrepancy in V1 attention effects results from the form of attention under study.
source: We believe that this apparent discrepancy results from the form of attention under study.
evidence: This is a direct statement providing an explanation for divergent findings.

claim: The study examines object-based attention with a superimposed design that excludes response modulation by space-based attention.
source: Here, we study object-based attention with a superimposed design that excludes response modulation by space-based attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design.

claim: Previous reports of significant attentional modulation in V1 include studies of space-based attention with stimuli presented at different locations.
source: Previous reports of significant attentional modulation in V1 include studies of space-based attention with stimuli presented at different locations (Somers et al., 1999; Gandhi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The effect of attention is less pronounced when the two stimuli are presented at the same location.
source: Considering the high reliance of V1 responses to location, the effect of attention is less pronounced when the two stimuli are presented at the same location, as is the case in the present study.
evidence: This is a direct statement providing an explanation for the V1 results.

claim: The current design may have led to an enhancement of the observed effect due to the predictability of target and distractor categories.
source: While it is possible that the current design has led to an enhancement of the observed effect, previous behavioral data Cohen et al., 2014; Xu and Vaziri-Pashkam, 2019 have reported the same effect in experiments in which the distractor was not predictable.
evidence: This is a direct statement acknowledging a potential limitation and citing previous work.

claim: Tuning sharpening, but not response gain, predicts the observed reduction in the effect of attention for more similar target-distractor pairs both at the univariate and at the multivariate level.
source: First, we demonstrate that tuning sharpening, but not response gain, predicts the observed reduction in the effect of attention for more similar target-distractor pairs both at the univariate and at the multivariate level.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the simulation results.

claim: A change in the tuning function improves attentional selection at high external noise levels.
source: Previous research has shown that a change in the tuning function improves attentional selection at high external noise levels (Ling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: A change in tuning function could lead to behavioral disadvantage in an environment where the target is not very different from the surrounding items.
source: Our results indicate that a change in tuning function could also lead to behavioral disadvantage in an environment where the target is not very different from the surrounding items.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: When attention is directed towards the target, the response to non-target objects that are more similar to the target is also enhanced, albeit to a lesser amount, leading to an overall weaker effect of attention for a more similar target-distractor pair.
source: When attention is directed towards the target, the response to non-target objects that are more similar to the target is also enhanced, albeit to a lesser amount, leading to an overall weaker effect of attention for a more similar target-distractor pair.
evidence: This is a direct statement explaining the mechanism.

claim: Tuning sharpening is suggested as the underlying mechanism in the domain of object-based attention.
source: Second, providing evidence from the human brain in favor of tuning sharpening, we suggest tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism in the domain of object-based attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proposed mechanism.

claim: The effects of attention have generally been explained by attention acting through increasing the contrast or response gain, especially for space-based attention.
source: The effects of attention have generally been explained by attention acting through increasing the contrast or response gain, especially for space-based attention (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004; Fox et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous research, supported by citations.

claim: A simple increase in gain cannot explain all reported effects of attention, and a change in the shape of the tuning curves has been observed during visual search and feature-based attention.
source: However, a simple increase in gain cannot explain all reported effects of attention, and a change in the shape of the tuning curves has been observed during visual search (Çukur et al., 2013), and feature-based attention (Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004; David et al., 2008; Ling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The speculation on the role of tuning sharpening in object-based attention is based on simulations and not neural data.
source: It is important to note that our speculation on the role of tuning sharpening in object-based attention is based on simulations and not neural data.
evidence: This is a direct statement acknowledging a limitation.

claim: To ascertain tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism for object-based attention, intracranial recordings from the human brain are needed.
source: To ascertain tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism for object-based attention, intracranial recordings from the human brain are needed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about future research needs.

claim: The results unravel the cortical basis by which target-distractor similarity affects attentional modulation.
source: In sum, our results unravel the cortical basis by which target-distractor similarity affects attentional modulation, and indicate tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism for response enhancement during object-based attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main conclusion.

claim: Tuning sharpening is indicated as the underlying mechanism for response enhancement during object-based attention.
source: In sum, our results unravel the cortical basis by which target-distractor similarity affects attentional modulation, and indicate tuning sharpening as the underlying mechanism for response enhancement during object-based attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main conclusion.
